title: network-landing-zone-patterns-and-upgrade-timeline-draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft that gathers recommended "landing zone" network patterns for private deployments (VPC and on-prem) and pairs them with an ops-friendly upgrade timeline for control-plane and dataplane changes. Aim is to provide a single quick-reference for solutions engineers and infra teams when preparing a new customer private deployment or planning an in-place runtime upgrade.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: SEs, Solutions Eng, infra engs doing customer VPC/on-prem onboarding, and the release team who coordinates upgrades.
- Scope: network topology patterns, high-level Terraform module boundaries and constraints, state/locking considerations, and a checklist + timeline template for rolling upgrades of Redwood Private control-plane and runtime stacks.

TL;DR (for SEs who just want bullet points):
- Start with one of three landing zone templates: "single-region-sandbox", "prod-multi-az-backplane", "onprem-hybrid-bridged".
- Keep Terraform modules small and composable: network, peering/Transit, vpn/expressroute, bastion/authn, infra-bootstrap. Avoid monolith module that touches both routing and KMS keys.
- Use remote state per-customer with workspace-per-environment and state-locking via S3+Dynamo or remote backend supported by customer (Artifactory/Equinix examples noted).
- Upgrades: plan a 6-week timeline for major runtime changes, 2-3 week for minor. Canary on a single customer and one internal staging tenant.

Reference landing zone patterns (high level):
1) single-region-sandbox (small customers / proof-of-concept)
   - /48 VPC (or whatever CSP recommends) with 2 private subnets + 1 public subnet for NAT/bastion.
   - Single AZ preference if customer constrained; document expected impact on SLA (no multi-AZ redundancy).
   - Simple NAT gateway (managed) or customer-managed Egress appliance depending on policy.
   - Recommended for early onboarding and debug windows.

2) prod-multi-az-backplane (recommended default for production)
   - Multi-AZ VPC with at least 3 private subnets (one per AZ) and multi-AZ NAT/IGW configuration.
   - Transit/Hub: recommend using cloud-native Transit Gateway / VPC Peering topology depending on scale. For >5 VPCs or hybrid connectivity, use Transit Gateway.
   - Dedicated route table per AZ and explicit local-only route for internal infra. Avoid broad 0.0.0.0/0 propagation in TGW attachments.
   - Security: default deny, explicit service fw rules for control-plane endpoints. Use mutual TLS for control-plane <-> runtime.

3) onprem-hybrid-bridged (air-gapped or partial on-prem)
   - Control plane (if customer requests private control plane) is hosted in customer network or on-prem colocation. Runtime can be on-prem or in customer VPC depending on needs.
   - Connectivity: prefer native Direct Connect / ExpressRoute + BGP with redundant paths. Use QoS for RTT-sensitive traffic.
   - If truly air-gapped: provide an offline installer artifact and helper scripts; we maintain staged releases and a checksum manifest.

Terraform module notes and boundaries (opinionated):
- module/ri-network: creates VPC, subnets, core route tables, core security groups, and tagging. Inputs: az_list, private_subnet_cidrs, public_subnet_cidrs, default_tgwrules. Outputs: subnet_ids, vpc_id, core_route_table_ids. Keep this module focused only on L3/L4 concerns.
- module/ri-connect: peering, TGW attachments, VPN/DirectConnect resources. Should accept an array of attachments with types and expected routing policy.
- module/ri-bastion: managed bastion host group + session manager configs (SSM / equivalent). Ideally implement as optional boolean switches to avoid forced EC2 in locked-down customers.
- module/ri-controlplane-endpoints: private endpoints (interface/privatelink) for control plane, DNS records, and ACM cert references.
- module/ri-bootstrap: small utilities that create IAM roles/service-accounts for infra automation, SSM parameters for secrets reference (NOT secrets themselves).
- Versioning: semantic (v0.x.y). Keep backwards-incompatible changes small and communicate via CHANGELOG + JIRA.

State and backend guidance:
- Use remote state per-customer and per-environment. Name pattern: redwood-<customer>-<env>-tfstate. Locking: DynamoDB or cloud-native locking mechanism.
- For on-prem customers without a remote backend, checkpoint: tarball of state and use manual apply with strict checklist. Avoid committing tfstate to any VCS.
- Secrets: do NOT store sensitive values in tfstate unless customer explicitly requests and accepts the risk; prefer referencing external secret manager.

Upgrade plan template (control-plane + runtime):
Phase 0 — Prep (weeks -4 to -2)
  - Create upgrade RFC (link to JIRA) and customer change window options.
  - Snapshot metrics baseline: latency p50/p95, token cost, error rates for last 30 days.
  - Validate infra — inventory of network resources, peerings, route tables.
  - Confirm TF state and drift report.

Phase 1 — Staging canary (week -2 to -1)
  - Apply changes to staging tenant that mirrors customer topology.
  - Smoke tests: inference correctness, auth, logs, metrics collection.
  - Run scale test at 10% of projected peak.

Phase 2 — Customer canary (week -1)
  - Schedule a 1-hour maintenance window with customer.
  - Apply minimal config first (control-plane lighter changes). Monitor for 2x expected window.
  - If issues: immediate rollback option documented (terraform rollback + restart services).

Phase 3 — Gradual rollout (week 0 to +1)
  - Apply changes to remaining clusters in rolling fashion AZ-by-AZ or cluster-by-cluster.
  - During each step run smoke and perf checks.
  - Validate cost & metrics post-change.

Phase 4 — Postmortem and followups (week +2)
  - Post-upgrade report, change in monitoring thresholds if needed.
  - Capture any manual remediation steps as permanent infra tasks in JIRA.

Checklist (quick):
- Backup current TF state (tag + encrypted copy).
- Document SSH/bastion creds and ensure access.
- Ensure customer has an emergency rollback contact and service window.
- Confirm KMS access and rotation impact.
- Confirm egress IPs and update allowlists if needed.

Operational notes and gotchas (lessons learned):
- Don't change route propagation + attach simultaneously — small step and verify.
- TGW cross-account propagation surprises: verify explicit route tables instead of assuming CAC.
- DNS for private endpoints: customers often forget split-horizon DNS; ensure we provide a how-to for private zone delegation.
- When using NAT gateway vs. carrier-grade egress box, document cost tradeoffs for heavy batch workloads (embedding generation spikes).
- For on-prem hybrid customers, clock skew and MTU mismatches are frequent sources of weird stability problems. Include MTU negotiation tests in acceptance.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- Decide standard default for NAT vs. egress appliance for "prod-multi-az-backplane" (ask infra cost analytics team).
- Add concrete terraform examples for indirect peering pattern (hub-> spoke route tables) — skeleton needed.
- Create automated drift report script and add as part of pre-upgrade checklist (JIRA: RI-1472).

Next steps (near-term):
- Convert this draft into a templated onboarding checklist that SEs can copy into customer folders.
- Promote modules to v0.4 with small refactor: split network and connect concerns.
- Wire up a Confluence page with diagrams (TGW vs Peering) and link into the onboarding playbook.

Notes:
- See linked GH PR for current module diffs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules/pull/87
- Related tickets: JIRA RI-1472 (upgrade automation), RI-1520 (private endpoint DNS delegation), RI-1599 (offline installer flow).

---
This doc is intentionally a working draft: expect shorthand, TODOs, and missing diagrams. Reach out to collaborators for diagram ownership and any immediate contradictions with current infra constraints.
